name: PA (Nylon / Polyamide)
chemical_makeup: Aliphatic polyamide — unfilled PA6 or PA12 semi-crystalline engineering thermoplastic. PA6 is stiffer, higher-melting and more hygroscopic; PA12 is lower density, absorbs less moisture and is more dimensionally stable at a lower melting point
summary: The toughest common engineering filament: outstanding layer adhesion, wear and impact resistance, and low friction, which is why it dominates gears, bushings and living mechanical parts. It is also the most demanding material here — extremely hygroscopic, high-warping, and dimensionally restless as humidity changes, so it needs constant drying, an enclosure and a forgiving build surface.

printing.notes: PA12 grades run roughly 240-290 °C (eSUN ePA12 TDS); PA6 grades usually 260-290 °C, and Prusa cites 285 °C for its PA blend. Keep part cooling near zero — aggressive cooling degrades layer adhesion and amplifies warping. An enclosure is effectively required for anything but small parts, and community practice targets ~45 °C+ ambient; an actively heated chamber is strongly beneficial for large parts but is not the hard prerequisite it is for PEEK-class polymers, so heated_chamber_required is recorded as false. Unfilled PA does not require a hardened nozzle, though stainless/hardened is commonly preferred; CF/GF-filled variants do require one.

feeding.notes: Mechanically unproblematic in a material station — Bambu's material table lists PA/PAHT as AMS-compatible — but nylon is the most hygroscopic material in this catalog, and an unsealed AMS-style unit is functionally an open-air spool holder. Over a long multi-material job an unsealed unit will let PA pick up enough moisture to string and bubble, so restrict it to a sealed, actively desiccated unit (AMS 2 Pro / AMS HT class) with fresh desiccant, or feed from a heated drybox instead. Third-party PA-CF and PA-GF are barred outright by Bambu because the fibres wear the AMS PTFE tubes. Enclosure: PA needs the retained chamber heat, so enclosure_open_for_cooling is false; Bambu specifies the cover installed for PA.

methods: print directly from a heated dryer
drying.dryness_validation: Clean, crisp extrusion with a glossy (not matte or fuzzy) surface finish; no audible popping or crackling at the nozzle; no steam, bubbles or foaming in the extrudate; stringing collapses back to normal; the snap-test brittleness of a saturated spool disappears
drying.notes: Nylon is the most hygroscopic common filament and degrades visibly — bubbling, stringing, brittleness — within hours of ambient exposure. eSUN specifies >12 h at 70 °C; Prusa says keep below 90 °C. Badly saturated spools can need 24-48 h. Printing from a heated dryer or sealed drybox is the practical default rather than an optional extra.

storage.recommendations: Airtight container with fresh desiccant at all times, including between prints on the same day; keep spools in a drybox on the printer rather than on an open shelf. Left in open air, nylon can absorb roughly 10% of its weight in water (Prusa).

price.notes: 2025-2026 unfilled PA6/PA12 pricing extrapolated from observed spool prices: budget eSUN lines ~$30-40/kg, Polymaker PolyMide CoPA ~$50-67/kg on 0.75-1 kg spools, specialist PA12 grades $55-90/kg. Precise current retail range unverified.

recommended: functional gears, bushings and low-friction bearings
tool handles, jigs and shop fixtures
end-use functional prototypes needing toughness and fatigue life
not_recommended: dimensionally critical precision fits without post-print conditioning
quick one-off prints (drying overhead outweighs the print)
parts under sustained load needing high stiffness and low creep

properties.notes: Density spans the PA12 (~1.01-1.04) to PA6 (~1.12-1.14) range; 1.08 is recorded as the mid-point for an unfilled generic PA. Tg is 40-60 °C depending on grade and drops further when the part is wet. HDT@0.45 MPa is the widest disagreement in the sources: eSUN ePA12 cites 100 °C while unfilled PA6 is often listed at 55-65 °C unless annealed — 80 °C is the recorded mid-point, not a datasheet value. Tensile: eSUN ePA12 50.8 MPa, partmfg table 52.45 MPa, general range 40-80 MPa. Snapmaker's Nylon spec page (owner-provided link, read 2026-08-06) publishes an unusually complete set for an undisclosed-grade PA: tensile 66.2 ± 0.9 MPa, bending 97.0 ± 1.1 MPa, Young's modulus 2223 ± 199 MPa, Charpy impact 9.6 ± 1.4 kJ/m², Tg 67 °C, Vicat 180 °C, melting point 190 °C, printing 250-270 °C, bed 25-50 °C, 30-60 mm/s. The Tg/melting pair is the informative part — Tg 67 °C is PA6-like while a 190 °C melt is nearer PA12 (~178 °C) than PA6 (~220 °C), which is the signature of a copolyamide rather than either homopolymer, and it is exactly why an unfilled-generic entry like this one has to average grades. No density, water absorption, shrinkage or drying schedule is published.

compatibility.notes: Nylon reliably welds only to itself. It does not bond usefully to pla, petg, abs, asa, pc, pp, pva, hips, bvoh, pctg, pvb or pet — the chemistry and the 240-290 °C print window are both mismatched. Some engineering TPUs are marketed as nylon-compatible and can reach marginal interlayer bonding, but that is brand-specific rather than a property of the class. Soluble supports are impractical: PVA degrades above ~200 °C and BVOH, while more heat-tolerant, still sits below nylon's range, so same-material PA breakaway supports are the standard workaround. PA is a poor support material for other polymers because it cross-bonds so weakly.

plate_recommendations.notes: Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): The headline use case. Multiple community reports state garolite prints nylon with no glue at all, where PEI plates need Magigoo PA or a glue stick. A thin PVA layer is optional pu

Textured PEI works at ~80-110 °C bed and is preferred over smooth PEI, which nylon can over-bond to and tear on removal. Adhesion on bare PEI is still inconsistent, so a glue stick is commonly applied as an adhesion PROMOTER here — the opposite of its release-layer role for PC/PETG/TPU. A dedicated PA sheet or garolite (G10) plate outperforms textured PEI for large parts.

emissions.notes: Caprolactam is the named marker compound for PA6 and has been reported at levels exceeding some chronic-exposure limits at close range in poorly ventilated spaces; Prusa's own knowledge base flags a strong odour. UFP emission is material- and temperature-dependent and sits between PLA's low baseline and ABS's high baseline. Use an enclosure plus active ventilation or a HEPA+carbon filter for extended prints, and do not run long nylon jobs in an unventilated occupied room.

safety_notes: Drying ovens set above 90 °C can deform spools and, at nylon's higher drying temperatures, accelerate off-gassing — keep drying under 90 °C and ventilate the dryer. Carbon- and glass-filled PA variants are abrasive and produce respirable fibre dust when sanded or machined; wear a respirator and use wet sanding.
additional_notes: Nylon parts continue to move after printing: they absorb ambient moisture and grow, then shrink again when dried, which is why precision fits should be conditioned (soaked to equilibrium or dried and sealed) before final measurement. Choosing between PA6 and PA12 is the main design decision — PA6 for stiffness and heat, PA12 for dimensional calm and easier printing. CoPA-class copolymer products migrated to the dedicated copa entry 2026-08-01.

provenance.conflicts: HDT@0.45 MPa is the largest unresolved disagreement: eSUN's ePA12 TDS cites 100 °C while unfilled PA6 is commonly listed at 55-65 °C unless annealed; 80 °C is a recorded mid-point rather than a measured figure. Density (1.01-1.14) and Tg (40-60 °C) both vary with PA6 vs PA12 grade rather than between sources, so single values here are grade-averaged. Nozzle temperature differs by grade: eSUN ePA12 240-290 °C vs Prusa's 285 °C for a PA blend. Price range is extrapolated from spool listings and is unverified against current retail. Max continuous service temperature (80-100 °C) is a community/aggregator figure, not a datasheet value. 2026-08-06 update (Snapmaker Nylon spec page — owner-provided link): NO recorded value changed. Confirmations: nozzle 250-270 °C sits inside the recorded 240-290 °C and straddles the recorded 265 °C recommendation; speed 30-60 mm/s sits inside the recorded 30-80 mm/s. Contradictions: tensile 66.2 ± 0.9 MPa is well above the recorded 52 MPa recommendation though still inside the recorded 40-80 MPa band — it is the highest unfilled-PA tensile figure seen here, above eSUN's ePA12 50.8 MPa and partmfg's 52.45 MPa, and it pulls the plausible centre of that band upward without justifying a move on one undisclosed-grade vendor sheet. Tg 67 °C is 17 °C above the recorded 50 °C and above the 40-60 °C grade range this entry describes, so the recorded Tg understates at least this grade. Bed 25-50 °C is dramatically colder than the recorded 70-110 °C with 90 °C recommended — a 20 °C gap at the ceiling. That is Snapmaker's own machine-tuned guidance on a small enclosed printer and it conflicts with every other nylon source in this entry; the recorded range is retained and the Snapmaker figure treated as an outlier, not a correction. HDT is not published by Snapmaker, so the entry's largest open disagreement (eSUN 100 °C vs unfilled PA6's 55-65 °C, recorded 80 °C) gets no help. No test method is cited.

alternatives.reason: The forgiving grade when this entry's warping and humidity drift are the problem: moisture uptake under 1 % against PA6's 3-9 % (water 7 vs 1), warp 6 vs 9 and dimensional stability 6 vs 3, with drying down to 70 °C/4 h — at lower stiffness (~45 vs 55-58 MPa) and a higher price ($55-90 vs $35-90).

The cheap, stiff homopolymer that most spools sold as generic 'PA' actually are ($35-70), if you want a named grade with published numbers — same punishing moisture and warp behaviour (warp 9, water 1) and no gain in printability (ease 3, equal).

The low-warp copolyamide: warp 3 vs 9 and dimensional stability 5 vs 3, so it prints far calmer while keeping nylon's best-in-family layer adhesion (9, equal) — but low warp is not low moisture (water 2 vs 1, still a 100 °C/8 h dry and sub-20 % RH storage) and it needs a hardened nozzle.

Carbon fiber collapses the warp (4 vs 9) and lifts HDT@0.45 MPa from ~80 °C to ~155 °C for $40-60/kg — at the cost of nylon's toughness (adhesion 4 vs 9), a mandatory hardened nozzle and no soluble-support option.

If the part just needs a tough, dimensionally stable plastic rather than nylon's wear, fatigue and low-friction behaviour, PETG skips the drying and the enclosure entirely (ease 7 vs 3, warp 3 vs 9, water 9 vs 1) at $18-42/kg.
